json.title: Transforming E. coli with a GFP plasmid
json.summary: Heat-shock competent E. coli with the pGLO plasmid, plate transformed and untransformed cells on LB, LB/ampicillin and LB/ampicillin/arabinose, grow them overnight, count colonies, look for fluorescence and calculate the transformation efficiency.
json.briefing: pGLO carries a gene for ampicillin resistance and the gene for green fluorescent protein, switched on by arabinose. Only cells that take up the plasmid can grow on ampicillin, and only those given arabinose should glow. Your control plates tell you whether your conclusions are sound.

json.title: Is it an operon? RT-PCR across gene junctions
json.summary: PCR on cDNA from E. coli grown with and without IPTG, with primers inside lacZ, lacY and lacA and across the junctions between them, a housekeeping gene (gapA), a no-RT control and genomic DNA, to show that lac is one inducible polycistronic mRNA.
json.briefing: cDNA is made from a cell's mRNA, so a PCR product from it shows the gene was transcribed. A primer pair spanning the junction of two genes gives a product from cDNA only if one mRNA covers both: an operon. gapA, transcribed in every cell, shows each cDNA worked; the no-RT control (RNA taken through without reverse transcriptase) shows whether genomic DNA in the RNA could give bands too; genomic DNA shows the junction primers work. Use 22 cycles so that differences in amount stay visible.

json.title: End-binding or coating? An agarose gel shift with two DNA lengths
json.summary: Titrate a Gam-like DNA-end-binding protein onto a supercoiled plasmid and onto 300 bp and 900 bp linear DNAs, run the reactions on an agarose gel, and from the shifts decide whether it needs DNA ends, whether it coats the DNA, and roughly how tightly it binds.
json.briefing: Protein bound to a DNA makes it run as a larger molecule: apparent mass = DNA mass + n × protein mass (660 g/mol per base pair; this protein 30.5 kDa a monomer). Compare the saturated shift of two lengths: a protein that sits only at the two ends gives the same n for both, one that coats the DNA gives n in proportion to length. Make a 3 µM working dilution for the lowest protein points.

concepts.label: Binding-site size from the saturated shift

json.title: What changed? Finding mutations and reversions by sequencing
json.summary: Sequence PCR products from two histidine-requiring Salmonella mutants and three of their revertants, find the mutated gene by searching reference sequences, read each mutation and each reversion from alignments, and spot a read from a mixed colony.
json.briefing: Each tube holds a PCR product of the his operon from one strain. Search a mutant's read against the references to find which gene it covers; align it with the best reference to see the change and what it does to the protein. A revertant grows without histidine again: align it with the reference and with its mutant to see whether the original change was undone, changed again, or compensated nearby.

json.title: A binding isotherm by EMSA: fitting the shift for an apparent Kd
json.summary: Titrate a DNA-binding protein onto a 900 bp linear DNA at eight concentrations, run the reactions on an agarose gel, measure how far each band has shifted relative to the free DNA, fit a Langmuir isotherm for the maximal shift and an apparent Kd, and judge the fit by its residuals.
json.briefing: The protein stock is 30 µM; a 3 µM working dilution serves the lowest points. In each lane the shift is 1 − (distance run) / (distance run by the free DNA, lane 3): 0 without protein, rising as protein loads onto the DNA. Fit shift = Rmax·[P]/(Kd + [P]).

objectives.statement: Set up a titration of binding reactions and run them on a gel

steps.prompt: Why fit shift = Rmax·[P]/(Kd + [P]) with two parameters rather than add a third (an offset)?

Three would be better: more parameters, better fit

steps.prompt: What do the residuals tell you about the fit?

options.label: They are small and scattered either side of zero with no trend: the isotherm describes the data
They trend systematically: the model is wrong

The concentration that saturates the DNA

json.title: Where does replication start? Origins, forks and the cell cycle from data
json.summary: Work out two microbes' genome structure, origins, fork speed, inter-origin distance and S phase from pulsed-field gels, ARS assays, replication profiles, DNA combing and flow cytometry, and decide which Earth organisms each resembles.
json.briefing: DNA fibres are stretched 2 kb per µm; the second (red) pulse lasted as recorded. Fork velocity = red track length / pulse time; inter-origin distance = spacing of neighbouring origins' centres.

objectives.statement: Interpret replication-origin and cell-cycle data
